entry.title: Quantumania 22 - Three Dimensions
entry.content:
When we first looked at the Hadamard gate there arose three matrices representing directions in physical space. They were introduced a little abruptly like background characters in someone else’s story, and they deserve some more spotlight. Here they are again:

\[Z = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \quad X = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad Y = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{bmatrix}\]

Geometrically they are all simply reflections. This is most obvious in MATHI5a, because they’re all written in the MATHI5a basis. MATHI5a just flips the sign of the second coordinate (the one that scales MATHI5c6b65747b317d) and has no effect on the first coordinate (the one that scales MATHI5c6b65747b307d). Or to put it another way, a vector of the form MATHI635c6b65747b307d, where MATHI63 is any complex scalar, is entirely unaffected:

\[Z c\ket{0} = c\ket{0}\]

whereas a vector of the form MATHI635c6b65747b317d experiences a sign-flip:

\[Z c\ket{1} = -c\ket{1}\]

So these, being only scaled by MATHI5a, are the eigenvectors of MATHI5a, whereas any other vectors will not only be scaled, they will be re-aligned. In general any state vector MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d can be written:

\[\ket{\psi} = a\ket{0} + b\ket{1}\]

The probability of measuring state MATHI5c6b65747b307d is MATHI61615e2a203d207c617c5e32, and for MATHI5c6b65747b317d it’s MATHI62625e2a203d207c627c5e32. But the act of multiplying (say) MATHI61 by its own complex conjugate has the effect of erasing any overall complex phase, because:

\[\left( e^{i\theta} \right)^* = e^{-i\theta}\]

and:

\[e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta} = e^{i\theta-i\theta} = e^0 = 1\]

This means that although MATHI5a flips the sign of MATHI5c6b65747b317d, this does not constitute an effect on anything physically significant about the state, because a sign flip is just a phase factor.

The other matrices represent the two orthogonal directions to MATHI5a. MATHI58 swaps the coordinates between MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI5c6b65747b317d, performing a reflection around the MATHI34355e5c63697263 line lying between them. This is the line that MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d sits on (if you’ve read the previous entries, you’ll be familiar with the diagram by now.) So MATHI5a has no effect at all on MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d, meaning that here MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d plays the same role that MATHI5c6b65747b307d played under MATHI5a. Likewise, a vector aligned with MATHI5c6b65747b2d7d would flip to point the opposite way. So if we were to rewrite all these matrices in the MATHI58 basis, then the MATHI58 matrix would have that same simple MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b646961677d28312c202d3129 form that we’ve given to the MATHI5a matrix.

MATHI59 is apparently the most exciting, in that it seems to combine both ingredients seen so far: a sign difference between the coordinates (like MATHI5a) and a swapping between the coordinates (off-diagonal entries only, like MATHI58), but to these it adds an overall factor of MATHI69. Again we can see how it affects its eigenvectors, which are given the mnemonic labels MATHI5c6b65747b2b697d and MATHI5c6b65747b2d697d to remind us of the coordinate on MATHI5c6b65747b317d:

\[\ket{+i} = \frac{\ket{0} + i\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}} \quad \quad \ket{-i} = \frac{\ket{0} - i\ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}}\]

Visualising this geometrically at first seems next to impossible (the MATHI5c6b65747b317d component has been scaled by a complex rotation that nevertheless doesn’t change its alignment), but based on the pattern so far, we’d expect MATHI59 to have no effect on MATHI5c6b65747b2b697d (we can ignore the overall MATHI5c667261637b317d7b5c737172747b327d7d because it appears on both sides of the equation):

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{bmatrix}\]

Check! Whereas it should perform an overall MATHI2d31 scale on MATHI5c6b65747b2d697d:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 0 & -i \\ i & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -i \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ i \end{bmatrix} = - \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{bmatrix}\]

All is as expected. In fact we can visualise it geometrically if we just relabel the axes on our usual diagram (come on, it’s been a while). When we use the MATHI5a-basis unit vectors MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI5c6b65747b317d to express the eigenvectors of MATHI58, we quietly ignored MATHI59, leaving it off the diagram. Well, now we can switch allegiance:

What is this voodoo?! Actually we’re still technically in the MATHI5a-basis here, because our vertical axis MATHI695c6b65747b317d is just as much of a valid eigenvector of MATHI5a as is MATHI5c6b65747b317d. Our diagrams have to be real subspaces of MATHI5c6d61746862627b437d5e32. We normally draw the real subspace spanned by MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b307d2c205c6b65747b317d205c726272616365, now we’re using the real subspace spanned by MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b307d2c20695c6b65747b317d205c726272616365.

In Bloch sphere terms, it gets even simpler. First, think of the usual MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b307d2c205c6b65747b317d205c726272616365 diagram. It is easily visualised as a circular slice through the Bloch sphere (with one important caveat). If you follow a point moving around that circle, it visits MATHI5c6b65747b307d, MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d, MATHI5c6b65747b317d, MATHI5c6b65747b2d7d in that order. Or to use their physical-space names instead of computing names, MATHI5c6b65747b757d (up), MATHI5c6b65747b667d (front), MATHI5c6b65747b647d (down), MATHI5c6b65747b627d (back):

There is no way to access MATHI5c6b65747b6c7d (left) MATHI5c6b65747b727d (right) from the provided ingredients if you are restricted to using only real coordinates to scale them. It’s the MATHI58-MATHI5a great circle, no MATHI59 ingredients are supplied, so the rest of the sphere is out of bounds. The caveat I mentioned is that the circle on the flat state space diagram is not precisely the same circle as this slice through the Bloch sphere, because MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI5c6b65747b317d are orthogonal in the state space, whereas in the corresponding Block sphere great circle they are antipodes (on opposite sides). The angle separating any two states is doubled on the Bloch sphere.

Now with MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b307d2c20695c6b65747b317d205c726272616365 as the axes of our state space diagram, we can access a great circle that visits MATHI5c6b65747b307d, MATHI5c6b65747b2b697d, MATHI695c6b65747b317d205c70726f70746f205c6b65747b317d, MATHI5c6b65747b2d697d, or MATHI5c6b65747b757d, MATHI5c6b65747b727d, MATHI5c6b65747b647d, MATHI5c6b65747b6c7d, never MATHI5c6b65747b667d or MATHI5c6b65747b627d. It’s MATHI59-MATHI5a only, and has no MATHI58 ingredients for us to scale with our strictly real coordinates:

Note how the state diagram’s MATHI695c6b65747b317d only differs by a phase factor (MATHI2d31) from MATHI5c6b65747b317d, so these refer to the same point on the Bloch sphere.

We’ve still only scratched the surface of this topic. For example, the matrices are reflections in 2-dimensional complex state space. What are they in the Bloch sphere, that is, in real 3-dimensional physical space?

entry.title: Quantumania 21 - Slot Machines
entry.content:
A ket is a “regular” vector, from the vector space MATHI56, a bra is a covector from the dual space MATHI565e2a (here I think QM has the upper hand, because almost everything is a vector, so it helps to have a specific term for a “regular” vector.)

A covector MATHI66 is a black box machine with one slot in the top, and you insert a vector MATHI5c7665637b617d, and out pops a scalar MATHI78:

It’s linear:

\[f(\vec{a} + \vec{b}) = f(\vec{a}) + f(\vec{b}) \quad \quad f(x \vec{a}) = x f(\vec{a})\]

We can add such machines (make a machine with one input slot, and internally it just feeds a copy of that input to two hidden machines and then sums their output scalars to produce the final output). Likewise we can scale a machine. The space of all such possible machines is a vector space MATHI565e2a. In QM we write such a machine as MATHI5c6272617b667d and have it operate on a vector MATHI5c6b65747b617d like this: MATHI5c6272616b65747b667d7b617d, and we define a one-to-one mapping between bras and kets. In general, that asterisk notation MATHI565e2a for the dual space of a space MATHI56 has nothing to do with complex conjugates. It’s a neat coincidence that the bra-ket mapping in a QM state space involves complex conjugation.

We can also make a machine with two slots, accepting vectors MATHI5c7665637b617d and MATHI5c7665637b627d, but still with one output hole that gives us back a scalar MATHI78:

Suppose that this two-slot machine had an especially simple inner mechanism: inside the box MATHI68 there are two single-slot boxes (covectors) MATHI66 and MATHI67. The machinery inserts input MATHI5c7665637b617d into box MATHI66, and input MATHI5c7665637b627d into box MATHI67, to obtain two scalars, which it simply multiplies together to produce its own resultant scalar that falls out of the hole of MATHI68. In other words, it’s really just two covectors glued together by scalar multiplication, and they act independently on the inputs. We can think of the tensor product on the input vectors as gluing them together in a specific order so it’s clear which slot each one is meant to go in:

\[\bra{h} = \bra{f} \otimes \bra{g}\] \[\bra{h} \Big( \ket{a} \otimes \ket{b} \Big) = \Big( \bra{f} \otimes \bra{g} \Big) \Big( \ket{a} \otimes \ket{b} \Big) = \braket{f}{a} \cdot \braket{g}{b}\]

This is a product machine, it’s behaviour explicable in terms of two separate inner machines. This is not true of all two-slot machines. Once again, these are vectors from a combined vector space, MATHI565e2a205c6f74696d657320565e2a. We can add a pair of two-slot machines to make another two-slot machine. Thus any two-slot machine might not be separable into two one-slot machines. It may only be expressible as the sum of multiple product machines. Or in QM terms:

\[\bra{\psi} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \bra{01} - \frac{1}{2} \bra{10}\]

The MATHI5c6272617b30317d203d205c6272617b307d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b317d and MATHI5c6272617b31307d203d205c6272617b317d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b307d are product machines, but their sum is not.

Note that it isn’t necessary to provide both inputs at once. Such a two-slot machine can be given one input, say for the first slot, which clogs up that slot, resulting in what is in effect a one-slot machine. Generalising further, the scalar that falls out after both inputs are provided is, in a sense, a zero-slot machine!

The symmetry of the notation where a bra acts on a ket to produce a scalar, MATHI5c6272616b65747b667d7b617d, can just as well be read as the ket acting on the bra; when implemented as a calculation in terms of coordinates, it has the same machinery as the familiar dot product: coordinate-wise multiplication to produce terms in a sum. So you can completely flip the picture around and visualise a ket as a one-slot machine that takes a bra as its input, and the tensor product of two kets as a two-slot machine, and so on.

We can even stitch together a two-slot machine from MATHI56205c6f74696d657320565e2a, that is, being defined conceptually through the combining of a ket and a bra (in that order), its inputs need to be a bra and a ket (again, in that order).

Wait a second… this is the shape of a projection operator! The QM notation MATHI5c6b65747b617d5c6272617b627d is itself a shorthand for MATHI5c6b65747b617d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b627d. When we write:

\[\ket{a}\braket{b}{c}\]

This is the operator MATHI5c6b65747b617d5c6272617b627d acting on the ket MATHI5c6b65747b637d, or we can say it’s the ket MATHI5c6b65747b637d being inserted into the second slot of the two-slot machine MATHI5c6b65747b617d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b627d.

So a term written like this in QM notation:

\[\ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1}\]

is building a four-slot machine. The two qubits MATHI41, MATHI42 have their own vector spaces MATHI565f41, MATHI565f42, so the four-slot machine is from the space:

\[V_A \otimes V_A^* \otimes V_B \otimes V_B^*\]

Now, given that the slots of these machines are either ket-shaped, expecting to be fed a bra, or bra-shaped and expecting to be fed a ket, its not that far-fetched to suppose that you could connect one of the slots to another! They just need to be slots of the opposite type, from the same dual-space pair, such as MATHI565f42 and MATHI565f425e2a, connected by a logical pipe of some kind. This is the so-called partial trace.

Once we adopt this way of thinking, we can completely forget about matrices altogether. There’s really only one bit of notation from classical physics (GR) that we haven’t yet borrowed, and it’s awfully tempting. Cast your mind all the way back up the page to when we wrote our joint state’s density operator as:

\[\sum_{i,k} \sum_{j,l} \rho_{ij,kl} \ket{i}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{j}\bra{l}\]

I made a big deal of how I’d written the indices clustered in a certain way to get across how they relate to which system versus bra/ket. There’s already a way to do this properly. The object MATHI5c72686f holding the coefficients for the MATHI3136 possible four-slot machines can be written:

\[\rho\indices{^i_k^j_l}\]

The indices are written “up” or “down” to signify the type of object they label, up for a ket and down for a bra. The way they’re laid means we can read one row at a time to separate ket from bra indices, or instead read columns (albeit slightly staggered) to group by qubit subsystem. It’s just a labelled collection of MATHI3136 numbers, with no inherent hierarchical matrix-of-matrices structure. We can slice it however it suits us.

Of course to interpret it properly we need to use each of these coefficients to scale a basis element, and rather than writing MATHI5c6b65747b697d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b6b7d205c6f74696d6573205c6b65747b6a7d205c6f74696d6573205c6272617b6c7d, we can represent a basis regular vector (ket) by MATHI5c7665637b657d5f69 (index down) and a basis covector (bra) by MATHI5c7665637b657d5e6a (index up). This opposing convention, where a coefficient and its corresponding basis element have oppositely positioned indices, has a purpose, which we’re about to get to.

\[\rho\indices{^i_k^j_l} \Big( \vec{e}_i \otimes \vec{e}^k \otimes \vec{e}_j \otimes \vec{e}^l \Big)\]

The final ingredients are the summation symbols, but here we come to what Einstein jokingly called his only contribution to mathematics. In an expression like the above where the same index appears twice, once up and once down, this automatically implies summation over that index. So the above expression is in fact the complete equivalent of our original way of writing it. The summation over all four indices is implied, so no need to write MATHI5c73756d at all.

We can go a step further and use abstract tensor notation, also known as the slot naming convention. This means we interpret MATHI5c72686f5c696e64696365737b5e695f6b5e6a5f6c7d not as merely a collection of labelled numeric coefficients, but as the full geometric object, the four-slot machine, silently agreeing to imagine that it has the MATHI5c7665637b657d5f69205c6f74696d6573205c646f7473 part built into it.

With this understanding, we’re writing the whole density operator for our two-qubit system as:

\[\rho\indices{^i_k^j_l}\]

Not only is this remarkably compact, it also means that if we want to “trace out” the second qubit, we just tie together its indices, which sit in the second column, by using the same symbol MATHI6a for both:

\[\rho\indices{^i_k^j_j} = (\rho_A)\indices{^i_k}\]

Because the MATHI6a index label appears once up and once down, it is summed over, eliminating those two slots, and this is precisely the same thing as the partial trace. We’re left with the density operator for qubit MATHI41, MATHI5c72686f5f41.

The implied basis vector factor MATHI5c7665637b657d5f69205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5e6b205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5f6a205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5e6a, also has the repeated MATHI6a index, and MATHI5c7665637b657d5f6a205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5e6a is equivalent to the identity operator, because it is summed over, and each term in the sum contributes a MATHI31 to the diagonal in the matrix representation, so it too disappears, leaving only the implied MATHI5c7665637b657d5f69205c6f74696d6573205c7665637b657d5e6b factor, exactly as required.

Let’s sum up. A density operator, MATHI5c72686f, can be simplistically viewed as a two-slot machine, where the slots accept a bra and a ket. Why such a pair? Taken together, they represent an input that accepts a density operator that acts as a kind of question to be asked.

So in the usual QM notation, we can write:

\[x = \bra{\phi} \rho \ket{\psi}\]

and MATHI78 is a scalar. Why the sandwich? Because the QM notation pays tribute to the pattern of matrix multiplication and the pieces have to be written in that order for such a multiplication to work. If we instead used explicit index notation:

\[x = \rho\indices{^j_k} \phi_j \psi^k\]

then we could write the factors in any order. The pairing of the indices describes a topological “wiring up” between connection points. Interpreting the factors as labelled coefficients, they are just numbers being multiplied, so clearly the order is unimportant. What matters is which combinations are multiplied and then summed. The result MATHI78 is still a scalar, because of the implied summation.

To supply a density operator to the slots is to ask a question. If we supply MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d5c6272617b5c7068697d, that’s a simple projection operator representing a specific state, and the question is: “What’s the probability that the system is in this state?” and MATHI78 is the answer.

The deeper point is that this two-slot case, while a valid way to describe any complex system, is a simplification if we are interested in the subsystems that comprise that complex system. Each subsystem can be thought of as having its own bra-ket pair of slots, and we can eliminate one subsystem by tying its slots together.

These two viewpoints are perfectly compatible because the tensor product allows us to connect the state spaces of any group of subsystems together into one state space. We can group them into a hierarchy, deal with them individually or all at once. If our system contains MATHI3130 qubits, we can divide them into three registers of MATHI32, MATHI33 and MATHI35 qubits each, each register exposing two slots. It’s vital to remember that they might not be three independent machines: their behaviour maybe correlated by entanglement.

entry.title: Quantumania 20 - Disentanglement
entry.content:
QM says the state of an isolated physical system is a well-defined thing, which I’ve characterised as sharp and definite, rather than blurry and uncertain, and which we’ve found two ways to represent: a vector in the state space, or a projection operator on that state space:

\[\ket{\psi} \quad \iff \quad \ket{\psi} \bra{\psi}\]

We can use the measurement operator for some measurement outcome (which can be as simple as the projection operator for the corresponding post-measurement state) to find the probability of an outcome, but that’s all. This implies some intrinsic uncertainty in how the universe works, sometimes called ontological probability, because the probability is aspect of the world, rather than just being due to our own lack of knowledge, which would be epistemic probability. If we attempt to measure some property, and the present state is not one of the post-measurement states associated with that property, we will nevertheless get a definite answer corresponding to one of the property’s post-measurement states, and it seems that nature chooses that answer at random. This is, in a sense, our own fault for asking the wrong question.

But the moment we measure an isolated system, it ceases to be isolated. Indeed, you could say that it never was isolated, as we were there the whole time too, along with the measuring equipment, all just subsystems of some larger system. This led us to consider composite state spaces accessed via the tensor product, which in turn led to the awkward realisation that sometimes the definite state of the composite system did not contain definite states for its subsystems. Only if the composite system is in a product state, meaning the tensor product of the states of the subsystems, can we regard the subsystem as having definite states of their own. To keep it much simpler than trying to model the state of ourselves, we’ll stick to just two qubits:

\[\ket{0} \otimes \ket{1} = \ket{01}\]

This is a product state, and is equivalent to saying that the first qubit is in MATHI5c6b65747b307d and the second is in MATHI5c6b65747b317d, so they can be thought of as possessing their own states. But this is a vector space; the sum of two vectors is also a vector, and so is also a physically real state, such as:

\[\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \ket{01} - \frac{1}{2} \ket{10}\]

It can’t be rewritten as a product, in any basis. It’s inherently the sum of two product states. It is possible for you to know exactly the state this whole system was prepared in, and yet still not know what state the individual qubits are in, not because of epistemic uncertainty, but because the two qubits don’t have a state of their own. There is nothing certain for you to know. The probability of measuring MATHI5c6b65747b30317d is MATHI332f34, and there’s a MATHI312f34 chance of measuring MATHI5c6b65747b31307d. This means that if you only measured the first qubit, MATHI332f34 times it’s MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI312f34 it’s MATHI5c6b65747b317d.

Here’s where the idea of a mixed state really becomes useful. We introduced it by considering boring old epistemic uncertainty, a coin flip whose result Bob doesn’t know. But we can use exactly the same approach to represent something like the actual state of one of the individual qubits, or the closest thing it has to a state. Its state is intrinsically mixed, in reality itself, not just in our minds because we lack information. The mixed description is all the information there is in the world about that one qubit.

We know what that mixed state would look like for the first qubit as a matrix, expressed in the MATHI5a basis, because we already worked out the probabilities:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \frac{3}{4} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{4} \end{bmatrix}\]

But this is only obvious because it’s a particularly simple setup. There is a proper way of getting from the density operator of a joint system to the density operator of one of its component subsystems that works even when the answer isn’t obvious. Our combined two-qubit system’s vector space is spanned by the usual basis vectors:

\[\lbrace \, \ket{00}, \ket{01}, \ket{10}, \ket{11} \, \rbrace\]

These are shorthands: MATHI5c6b65747b30317d203d205c6b65747b307d205c6f74696d6573205c6b65747b317d and so on. There is a corresponding bra-space:

\[\lbrace \, \bra{00}, \bra{01}, \bra{10}, \bra{11} \, \rbrace\]

These are operators that act on a ket to produce a scalar, the inner product. Or we can write them in reverse as a ket-bra to make all the elementary projection operators (or in matrix form, matrices whose entries are all zero except for a single MATHI31, which can be scaled and added to make any matrix.)

Through the tensor product, the parts of an operation related to one subsystem “find each other” and act independently. We saw exactly this when we applied the Hadamard operator MATHI485e7b5c6f74696d6573206e7d to a whole register of MATHI6e qubits: it’s the same as applying Hadamard to each qubit individually. So these are equivalent:

\[\ket{i}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{j}\bra{l} = \ket{ij} \bra{kl}\]

So even if we aren’t certain of our joint two-qubit system’s state, and we have to describe it as a density operator rather than a pure state, that’s fine:

\[\sum_{i,k} \sum_{j,l} \rho_{ij,kl} \ket{i}\bra{k} \otimes \ket{j}\bra{l}\]

Here the MATHI69, MATHI6a, MATHI6b and MATHI6c indices range over MATHI5c6c627261636520302c2031205c726272616365, so they are the usual qubit basis state labels. Thus MATHI5c72686f5f7b696a2c6b6c7d symbolises the 16 coefficients of the joint state’s density matrix MATHI5c72686f, each giving a weighting to the tensor product of two single-qubit density operators. MATHI69 and MATHI6a label the kets, while MATHI6b and MATHI6c label the bras.

The exact way we’ve split the indices into different summations carries a significance, even though we could have written them many different ways. Ultimately we need all 16 combinations of the possible index values. But it makes sense to bunch them by which subsystem (qubit) they are driving. To see why, check out the almighty mess we get when we tabulate all the terms of the above sum:

\[\begin{matrix} & k=0, l=0 & k=0, l=1 & k=1, l=0 & k=1, l=1 \\ i=0, j=0 & \rho_{00,00} \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{0} & \rho_{00,01} \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1} & \rho_{00,10} \ket{0}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{0} & \rho_{00,11} \ket{0}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1} \\ i=0, j=1 & \rho_{01,00} \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{0} & \rho_{01,01} \ket{0}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{1} & \rho_{01,10} \ket{0}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{0} & \rho_{01,11} \ket{0}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{1} \\ i=1, j=0 & \rho_{10,00} \ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{0} & \rho_{10,01} \ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1} & \rho_{10,10} \ket{1}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{0} & \rho_{10,11} \ket{1}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{0}\bra{1} \\ i=1, j=1 & \rho_{11,00} \ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{0} & \rho_{11,01} \ket{1}\bra{0} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{1} & \rho_{11,10} \ket{1}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{0} & \rho_{11,11} \ket{1}\bra{1} \otimes \ket{1}\bra{1} \\ \end{matrix}\]

In each cell we write both the first and second qubit’s ket-bra, stitched together with the tensor product, and also scaled by the coefficient MATHI5c72686f5f7b696a2c6b6c7d that would appear in the density matrix. MATHI69 and MATHI6a drive the rows, whereas MATHI6b and MATHI6c drive the columns.

It’s tricky to spot any pattern to it, but the way we grouped the summation variables doesn’t follow this ket/bra, row/column picture, and this is deliberate:

\[\sum_{i,k} \sum_{j,l}\]

Instead, it divides the labels according to subsystem: MATHI69 and MATHI6b produce the first qubit, MATHI5c6b65747b697d5c6272617b6b7d, whereas MATHI6a and MATHI6c produce the second, MATHI5c6b65747b6a7d5c6272617b6c7d.

The first qubit’s four basis states each relate to one of four quadrants of the table, visited in turn by the MATHI5c73756d5f7b692c6b7d summation. The second qubit lives inside each quadrant as its four entries, visited by MATHI5c73756d5f7b6a2c6c7d. Breaking it down into these quadrants and ignoring the details of the second qubit:

\[\begin{array}{c|c} i=0, k=0 & i=0,k=1 \\ \hline i=1, k=0 & i=1,k=1 \\ \end{array}\]

So there’s a hierarchy to it: the outer structure of quadrants describing the first qubit, the inner entries of each quadrant describing the second qubit. To distil it down to a MATHI32205c74696d65732032 density matrix for the first qubit, we just need “blur our eyes”, turning the details of each quadrant into a single number. This is what the trace does, but here we’re applying it separately to each quadrant, and it’s called the partial trace:

\[\sum_{i,k} \sum_{j,l} \rho_{ij,kl} \ket{i}\bra{k} \cdot \operatorname{Tr} \Big( \ket{j}\bra{l} \Big)\]

Recall that MATHI5c6b65747b6a7d, being a basis vector, is a one-hot column. The outer product MATHI5c6b65747b6a7d5c6272617b6c7d in matrix form only ever has MATHI31 in a single entry, the rest being MATHI30, and this single MATHI31 will only sit on the main diagonal if MATHI6a203d206c. This means that the trace is MATHI31 if MATHI6a203d206c and is MATHI30 otherwise, and further means that any term in our summation where MATHI6a205c6e65206c will vanish. This gets rid of half the terms automatically.

Now, if you’re familiar with tensors as they appear in classical physics, you may be wondering why this isn’t just referred to as contraction, and I think you have a point! It is literally just an example of that. QM has its own terminology. Also, the hierarchical arrangement of the two subsystems is completely arbitrary, a byproduct of using matrix notation, and obscures more than it illuminates in my opinion. We don’t have to do it this way.

entry.title: Quantumania 19 - Disappear With Trace
entry.content:
Last time we discovered projection operators, starting with the ket-bra or outer product:

\[\ket{\phi} \bra{\phi}\]

which operates on a vector MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d by projecting it onto MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d, i.e. scaling MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d by the inner product MATHI5c6272616b65747b5c7068697d7b5c7073697d:

\[\ket{\phi} \braket{\phi}{\psi}\]

It may have occurred to you that such an operator can be thought of as an alternative representation of MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d. Rather than representing states as vectors in a vector space, perhaps we could instead represent them with operators acting on that vector space. This is appealing in that it means we represent everything through operators: states, transformations, measurements.

The downside is that it seems a little wasteful when you think about the numerical description of a qubit state in some basis as now requiring four numbers instead of two. But consider also that if we take a representation of MATHI5c6b65747b5c7068697d in some basis as having two coordinates MATHI285c7068695f312c205c7068695f3229, then the outer product produces a matrix:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \phi_1 \\ \phi_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \phi_1^* & \phi_2^* \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \phi_1 \phi_1^* & \phi_1 \phi_2^* \\ \phi_2 \phi_1^* & \phi_2 \phi_2^* \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \vert \phi_1 \vert^2 & \phi_1 \phi_2^* \\ \phi_2 \phi_1^* & \vert \phi_2 \vert^2 \end{bmatrix}\]

The diagonal elements are always real, being the modulus squared of some complex number. Furthermore, assuming the basis is aligned with the eigenvectors of some observable, they are the probabilities of obtaining distinguishable measurement outcomes. Also they are all such probabilities, so they must sum to MATHI31.

We’ve talked before about state vectors needing to be unit vectors so that when we interpret their coordinates as complex amplitudes, and take the modulus-squared, we get probabilities. By switching to projection operators as our states, we can replace that requirement by instead saying that the sum of the diagonal entries of the state’s projection operator must be MATHI31. This aspect of a matrix is important enough to have a name, the trace, MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b54727d284d29. When we think about matrices we can remember it simply as the sum of the diagonal entries. But perhaps surprisingly, it does not depend at all on our choice of basis. This means we’re not merely talking about the trace of a matrix specific to some numerical representation; we’re talking about the trace of an operator, an invariant basis-independent fact.

To see why, albeit it in a rather laborious way to begin with, recall that to convert a matrix to another orthogonal basis is simply to place it in the sandwich of rotation and un-rotation, MATHI55204d20555e7b2d317d. The rotation takes the form:

\[U = \begin{bmatrix} x & -y^* \\ y & x^* \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{where } \vert x \vert^2 + \vert y \vert^2 = 1\]

That restriction on the sum of the squares is equivalent (in real vector spaces) to saying:

\[x = \cos \theta \quad \quad \quad y = \sin \theta\]

but we can put that out of our minds. More importantly, the inverse MATHI555e7b2d317d is the adjoint MATHI555e5c646167676572. Let’s make the basis-conversion sandwich around some matrix MATHI4d with any old entries:

\[M = \begin{bmatrix} j & k \\ l & m \end{bmatrix}\]

and multiply it on the left and then on the right:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} M' &=& U M U^\dagger \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} x & -y^* \\ y & x^* \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} j & k \\ l & m \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x^* & y^* \\ -y & x \end{bmatrix} \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} jx - ly^* & kx - my^* \\ jy + lx^* & ky + mx^* \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x^* & y^* \\ -y & x \end{bmatrix} \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} jxx^* - lx^*y^* - kxy + myy^* & \dots \\ \dots & jyy^* + lx^*y^* + kxy + mxx^* \end{bmatrix} \end{eqnarray*}\]

I haven’t bothered to write in the off-diagonal entries at the end because we only want the trace, MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b54727d284d2729, so we add the main diagonal entries:

\[\begin{align*} \operatorname{Tr}(M') &=& \left( jxx^* - lx^*y^* - kxy + myy^* \right) + \left( jyy^* + lx^*y^* + kxy + mxx^* \right) \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}gather like terms:} &=& \left(jxx^* + jyy^* + mxx^* + myy^* \right) + \left(lx^*y^* - lx^*y^* + kxy - kxy \right) \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}cross terms cancel:} &=& jxx^* + jyy^* + mxx^* + myy^* \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}but $xx^* = \vert x \vert^2$ so:} &=& j\vert x \vert^2 + j\vert y \vert^2 + m\vert x \vert^2 + m\vert y \vert^2 \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}pull out common factors:} &=& j\left( \vert x \vert^2 + \vert y \vert^2 \right) + m \left(\vert x \vert^2 + \vert y \vert^2 \right) \\ \shortintertext{\small\color{gray}but $\vert x \vert^2 + \vert y \vert^2 = 1$ so:} &=& j + m = \operatorname{Tr}(M) \end{align*}\]

The trace is unaffected by the change of basis. It is a fact about the operator described by the matrix, not merely a fact about the specific representation of that operator as a matrix in a particular basis.

Though there’s actually a much simpler way to reach this conclusion. Never mind rotations, consider any three matrices being multiplied together (again we only need the main diagonal entries):

\[\begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} j & k \\ l & m \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} paj + qcj + pbl + qdl & \dots \\ \dots & kar + ksc + mbr + msd \end{bmatrix}\]

Fine. But what do we get if we cycle the three inputs around so the first one moves to third place, second becomes first and third becomes second?

\[\begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} j & k \\ l & m \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} p & q \\ r & s \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} paj + pbl + kar + mbr & \dots \\ \dots & qcj + qdl + ksc + msd \end{bmatrix}\]

All the same terms are there, just switched around a bit, but that won’t affect the trace. So for any matrices MATHI412c20422c2043:

\[\operatorname{Tr}(ABC) = \operatorname{Tr}(BCA)\]

This is the cyclic property of the trace. And therefore, as MATHI555e5c6461676765722055203d2049:

\[\operatorname{Tr}(U M U^\dagger) = \operatorname{Tr}(M U^\dagger U) = \operatorname{Tr}(M)\]

So now we’ve got two interesting facts about traces, in addition to the QM rule that for a projection operator MATHI50 representing a state, MATHI5c6f70657261746f726e616d657b54727d285029203d2031. But we’re still waiting for the states-as-operators idea to really earn its keep by doing something new.

Okay, new scenario. Alice is sending Bob a qubit, and it’s either MATHI5c6b65747b307d or MATHI5c6b65747b317d, and she flips a coin to decide which. So is this a description of the state of the qubit?

\[\ket{+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{0} + \ket{1} \Big)\]

Nope. That’s a qubit state that Alice is definitely not going to send. All the way back at the start we swore never to be wishy washy and always remember that a state is a sharply defined arrow, and if you think of it as a superposition that’s a matter of interpretation. What we have here is sometimes called classical uncertainty. Put more simply, we know Alice is going to send one of two states, we don’t know which one, but we know they’re equally likely.

We can represent this state of knowledge (which is not the same thing as a state as we’ve been using that term so far) by weighting each state projection operator by its probability and adding the results:

\[\frac{1}{2} \ket{0} \bra{0} + \frac{1}{2} \ket{1} \bra{1} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{2} & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\]

We can see that this is entirely different from the projection operator for MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d:

\[\ket{+}\bra{+} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{2} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

So a matrix can describe our state of knowledge when it has some uncertainty about it, and in this case it’s a different thing from the so-called quantum uncertainty we hear about. There is a fact in the world, and Alice knows that fact, but Bob doesn’t. Alice and Bob would each make a different matrix to describe their own state of knowledge.

Alice would describe her state of knowledge with a pure state, a projection operator that is equivalent to a definite state vector. Bob would describe his state of knowledge with a mixed state (in this context a somewhat misleading term), which is the sum of all the possible pure state matrices, each weighted by its probability. The collective term for these is a density operator, after the classical concept of a probability density function, although it’s more common to hear the matrix representation of such an operator referred to as a density matrix.

But there’s a much more interesting application of these ideas, one which ties together much of the themes we’ve been wrestling with, even the dreaded measurement problem.

entry.title: Quantumania 18 - Mixed Messages
entry.content:
We’ve considered measurable things, such as which way something is pointing in space, and the framework we’ve given for that implied that the only kinds of physical measurement we can do involve measuring in one basis. That is, all the possible outcomes of the measurement correspond to orthogonal state vectors, giving us a very convenient basis in which to capture the state vector in coordinates, such that each coordinate gives us one of the outcomes.

Another way to write this is as follows. If MATHI5c6b65747b4d5f6e7d is the vector associated with the MATHI6e-th measurement outcome, and clearly our state vector MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d can be thought of as a column vector written in the basis MATHI5c6c6272616365205c6b65747b4d5f317d2c205c6b65747b4d5f327d205c646f7473205c726272616365, then:

\[\braket{M_n}{\psi}\]

in effect means “pluck the MATHI6e-th coordinate out of MATHI5c707369”.

Recalling that if you switch the labels on a bra-ket it’s the complex conjugate, and to convert the MATHI6e-th coordinate into the probability of obtaining the MATHI6e-th measurement outcome we need to multiply it by its own complex conjugate, that probability can be written:

\[\braket{\psi}{M_n} \braket{M_n}{\psi}\]

But we’ve written it in a way that doesn’t assume anything about a coordinate representation in any basis. We’re using operations with a geometrical meaning: the inner product of two vectors, which is invariant, completely independent of the choice of basis. We know our state vector could be described in the measurement basis, that is, there must be some column of complex coordinates MATHI635f6e such that:

\[\ket{\psi} = \sum_n \ket{M_n} c_n\]

And we can use the inner product to get those coordinates, MATHI635f6e203d205c6272616b65747b4d5f6e7d7b5c7073697d. Substituting:

\[\ket{\psi} = \sum_n \ket{M_n} \braket{M_n}{\psi}\]

In that expression our eye is naturally drawn to the familiar bra-ket pattern, which we should be in the habit of seeing as a scalar. So the expression inside the sum builds a vector that is colinear with MATHI5c6b65747b4d5f6e7d, as that’s what we’re scaling. But let’s pull out this part by itself:

\[\ket{M_n} \bra{M_n}\]

We could call this a ket-bra, I guess? Nobody does though. Given that the bra-ket’s official name is the inner product, it’s easy to remember the ket-bra’s official name, the outer product. The role played by this object in our example is to operate on a vector to product another vector, and so it’s an operator and can be represented by a matrix. In fact, if we have a column vector representing MATHI5c6b65747b4d5f6e7d, and we use the hermitian conjugate to get a row vector representing MATHI5c6272617b4d5f6e7d, writing them side-by-side in ket bra order is simply matrix multiplication:

\[P_n = \ket{M_n} \bra{M_n} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} a \\ b \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} a^* & b^* \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} a a^* & a b^* \\ b a^* & b b^* \end{bmatrix}\]

So for the basis vectors in the measurement basis:

\[P_1 = \ket{M_1} \bra{M_1} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad P_2 = \ket{M_2} \bra{M_2} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

These are called projection operators, because when applied to a vector MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d, they project it onto the vector they were built from. MATHI505f31 flattens a vector into alignment with MATHI5c6b65747b4d5f317d, making the component vector of MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d along MATHI5c6b65747b4d5f317d, or MATHI635f31205c6b65747b4d5f317d where MATHI635f31 is the first coordinate of MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d in the MATHI4d basis. So if used like this:

\[\bra{\psi} P_n \ket{\psi} = \braket{\psi}{M_n} \braket{M_n}{\psi} = c_n^* c_n\]

So we go straight to the probability of obtaining the MATHI6e-th measurement outcome from state MATHI5c6272617b5c7073697d. Why bother to think of the middle operator as new type of thing? Because this allows us to generalise the idea of a measurable outcome to include non-orthogonal possibilities. Measuring equipment isn’t always as ideal as we might imagine.

Even so, we can see how this looser way of defining measurement can be applied if we imagine a scenario that is still idealised, but in a different way to usual. Suppose Alice is going to receive (from Bob, of course) a qubit and all she knows is that its state is going to be either MATHI5c6b65747b307d or MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d. That is, either a basis state of the Z basis, or a basis state of the X basis. Welcoming back our old friend (don’t worry, there’s a whole new diagram coming up):

These two possibilities are not orthogonal. They’re at MATHI34355e5c63697263 to one another. Each is a basis vector of one basis that can be expressed as a balanced superposition of the other basis.

If Alice measures in the Z basis she might find MATHI5c6b65747b317d. As she knows Bob definitely didn’t send her that, she can conclude he definitely sent MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d and it just flipped randomly into the MATHI5c6b65747b317d state. If he’d sent the other option, MATHI5c6b65747b307d, she would have measured that with certainty, because it’s a basis vector of the basis she’s measuring in.

But if she finds MATHI5c6b65747b307d, what does that tell her? Bob could have sent her MATHI5c6b65747b307d, but equally he could have sent MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d and it flipped into MATHI5c6b65747b307d, as it randomly might. She could reason in much the same way about a measurement on the X basis. Whichever basis she chooses to measure in, the outcome is certain for one of the possibilities, occurring half the time (assuming Bob makes an unbiased random choice of what to send), and “Who knows?” for the other half.

The only way to improve on this is to make a trade-off: to accept getting a “Who knows?” answer more than half the time, but in exchange sometimes getting an absolutely certain answer for whichever qubit Bob sends. Mathematically the core of this is the orthogonal complement.

To picture this, think of a plane surface, orientated at some interesting angle. Then think of light rays shining on it so they are perfectly perpendicular to the plane. Now imagine a stick attached to the plane and sticking out from it. If the stick is itself perpendicular to the plane it won’t cast a shadow, because it’s in line with the light rays. But if the stick is tilted away from the perpendicular, it will cast a shadow. The shadow is the stick’s component in the plane.

We can think of this as a 3D vector space if we visualise the origin as the point where the stick is attached to the plane. How can a plane exist in a vector space? Easy: it’s a set of vectors. The plane is a 2D subspace of the 3D space, containing all the vectors that lie in the plane.

We can turn the stick into the shadow by applying a projection operator that flattens 3D vectors into that 2D subspace. To construct that operator, suppose we know the vector MATHI5c6b65747b767d that is normal (orthogonal) to the plane, that is, it’s orthogonal to any vector lying in the plane. This is the vector that wouldn’t cast any shadow. Then we work out this operator:

\[I - \ket{v} \bra{v}\]

It’s the projection operator on to MATHI5c6b65747b767d subtracted from the identity operator. So if we represent all this in coordinates such that MATHI5c6b65747b767d is the first basis vector:

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}\]

The resulting matrix very clearly discards the first coordinate (the MATHI5c6b65747b767d direction) but retains the information from the other two (the plane), so flattens whatever vector it applies to into its shadow on the plane. And if applied a second time to that shadow, it will have no effect. The shadow exists in the 2D plane that is represented by the MATHI32205c74696d65732032 square matrix in the lower right, which looks uncannily like the 2D identity matrix, because it is. To qualify as a projection operator, we only require that an operator is:

  • hermitian (self-adjoint): MATHI505e5c646167676572203d2050
  • idempotent: MATHI505e32203d2050 (if applied a second time, it makes no difference, the damage is done.)

Now, in our example with qubits the space is two dimensional, so projection operators can only project onto lines, not planes.

\[\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}\]

So in 2D, the orthogonal complement of a vector is not a plane, it’s just another vector, although it is orthogonal to the original. But I wanted to get across the general idea as it pertains to higher dimensional vector spaces because that’s what we’re dealing with when we have more than one qubit.

Also, bear in mind that the kind of measurement we’re going to talk about next makes use of orthogonal complements to projection operators, which are themselves projection operators, and yet the official term “projective measurement” is reserved for the kind of measurement we’ve previously talked about, where we choose a basis to measure in, and the probabilities of obtaining the outcomes are found by projecting the state vector onto the basis vectors.

Back to Alice and Bob. Alice wants three measurement outcomes: two are definite answers: MATHI5c6b65747b307d or MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d, and the other is “don’t know.” It’s okay if she gets a lot of don’t-knows, as long as she never gets a confidently wrong answer.

By sending the qubit through certain purely unitary transformations, it is possible to effectively send it into the path of three detectors, each of which does an ordinary projective measurement (that is, measuring in a specific basis just as we’ve always talked about), but only one of the three detectors will actually detect something, because although we can’t say anything for sure about how the qubit travels to its destination, it ultimately “collapses” to one of the three possible destinations. Alice makes it so that one of the detectors has zero probability of detecting something if the input qubit was MATHI5c6b65747b307d, another has zero probability for MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d, and the third mops up the remaining probability.

More precisely, the first detector’s probability of firing for a qubit in state MATHI5c6b65747b5c7073697d is:

\[\bra{\psi} E_1 \ket{\psi}\]

where

\[E_1 \propto I - \ket{0} \bra{0}\]

(Note that it’s proportional-to, rather than equal-to: there would be an overall scaling factor to make sure the probabilities add to MATHI31.)

The projection MATHI455f31 obliterates any component in the MATHI5c6b65747b307d direction. If the qubit is exactly MATHI5c6b65747b307d, it has a zero-length shadow in this projection. There’s a similar MATHI455f32 that obliterates MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d. Finally, the don’t-know detector is just:

\[E_? = I - (E_1 + E_2)\]

It’s the complement of the sum of the other two complements: it throws away that which would cause the either of the other two to cast a shadow.

So Bob sends MATHI5c6b65747b307d, detector 2 is the only one that definitely won’t fire. If he sends MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d, detector 1 cannot fire. Either way, detector 3 always has a probability of firing, so Alice will get a lot of don’t-knows. But if detector 1 fires, she knows for absolute certain that Bob sent MATHI5c6b65747b307d, and if 2 fires she knows he sent MATHI5c6b65747b2b7d.

entry.title: Quantumania 17 - More Function, More Mystery
entry.content:
We ended up being slightly less impressed than we might have been about the Hadamard gate’s ability to narrow down the identity of a mystery function from four possibilities to two with a single measurement, given that we could make the same amount of progress by invoking the function once directly. If you give the function MATHI30 as the input, it can only output MATHI30 or MATHI31, and that divides the four possible functions into two pairs.

Even so, there’s still something neat about the idea that we’ve “rotated a function” so that we can, with a single invocation, narrow it down to being either a constant that ignores its input or being dependent on its input, something that seems to absolutely require two invocations. I used the term balanced for the latter kind, in anticipation of the upgrade we’re going to embark on today.

That upgrade is going to show off our ability to casually string together many qubits into a register of qubits. I think it’s quite cool that we’re using terminology from classical computing. Registers in this context, as in mechanisms for temporarily storing numbers, have existed for as long as mechanical calculators (hundreds of years.) A long time ago there was something called a cash register (ask your grandma.)

We can build states for compound systems of three qubits by using the tensor product to stitch their spaces together:

\[\ket{0} \otimes \ket{0} \otimes \ket{0} = \ket{000}\]

Rather than writing out absurdly long kets as we increase the number of qubits to a large number MATHI6e, you’ll sometimes see this notation:

\[\ket{0} ^{\otimes n}\]

We’re just raising MATHI5c6b65747b307d to the power of MATHI6e (but using the tensor product.) So that’s a really quick way to say I have a system of MATHI6e qubits. Now, with such a system I can apply a unitary operation like Hadamard (symbolised here by MATHI48) to individual qubits:

\[H \ket{0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{0} + \ket{1} \Big)\]

If I have two qubits in MATHI5c6b65747b307d and put each through Hadamard, and multiply out:

\[H \ket{0} \otimes H \ket{0} = \frac{1}{2} \Big( \ket{0} + \ket{1} \Big) \Big( \ket{0} + \ket{1} \Big) = \frac{1}{2} \Big( \ket{00} + \ket{01} + \ket{10} + \ket{11} \Big)\]

Now for the first time (it’s a big day) we’re actually going to interpret the bit patterns in qubit tensor products as actual binary numbers. What happens if we have a system of MATHI38 qubits, in which MATHI5c6b65747b30303130313031307d would signify MATHI3432, but ours are initially all zero, and put each them through Hadamard and multiply out?

\[\frac{1}{16} \Big( \ket{00000000} + \ket{00000001} + \ket{00000010} + \cdots \ket{11111101} + \ket{11111110} + \ket{11111111} \Big)\]

It’s an equal superposition of every number in the range MATHI30 to MATHI323535. Why is the normalisation factor MATHI312f3136? Because this is Pythagoras in MATHI323536 dimensions: all those ingredients are unit vectors, the square of the length of each is MATHI31, there are MATHI323536 of them, so the square of the “hypotenuse” of this ultra-hyper-bonkers-triangle is MATHI323536, thus its length is MATHI5c737172747b3235367d203d203136, so that’s what we need to divide by to shrink it down to MATHI31.

In general, for MATHI6e qubits treated in this way the result is the state vector:

\[\ket{\psi} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}} \sum_{x = 0}^{2^n - 1} \ket{x}\]

Here MATHI78 can be thought of the value between MATHI30 and MATHI325e6e202d2031 but represented in binary and used as the label for one of the ingredients.

Now we have what we need to upgrade our mystery function scenario so that function takes an MATHI6e-bit number as its input and produces a single bit as output. But to make this work we’re going to have to introduce a restriction on the mystery function that will seem a little contrived: it either ignores the input number entirely (it’s a constant), or it is balanced, meaning that for exactly half the range of possible values it produces output MATHI31 and for the other half MATHI30. Supposing it is balanced, we have no idea which input values produce MATHI31. To be sure it’s not constant, you’d have to test the function on just over half the possible input values, MATHI325e6e2f32202b2031, potentially a huge number.

When we had one-bit input, the mystery function was wrapped in a unitary operator, by passing the first qubit straight through unchanged (at least, according to the definition) and using the result of the function to affect the second qubit’s output.

\[U_f \ket{A, B} = \ket{A, B \oplus f(A)}\]

Now we’re going to do the same thing except MATHI41 is our qubit register, carrying some MATHI6e-bit number. MATHI42 is just an extra qubit that will carry the encoded output, and at input it is MATHI48205c6b65747b317d203d205c6b65747b2d7d, so the complete input state is:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}} \sum_{x = 0}^{2^n - 1} \ket{x} \otimes \ket{-}\]

When MATHI555f66 acts on this, being linear, it distributes over all the summed terms. Each term is in effect acted on like this:

\[U_f \Big( \ket{x} \otimes \ket{-} \Big) = U_f \left( \ket{x} \otimes \frac{\ket{0} - \ket{1}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{0 \oplus f(x)} - \ket{x} \ket{1 \oplus f(x)} \Big)\]

This means that if MATHI66287829203d2030, it adds nothing and this particular term is unchanged:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{0 \oplus f(x)} - \ket{x} \ket{1 \oplus f(x)} \Big) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{0} - \ket{x} \ket{1} \Big) = \ket{x} \otimes \ket{-}\]

Whereas if MATHI66287829203d2031 it in effect swaps the labels of the output bit ingredients:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{0 \oplus f(x)} - \ket{x} \ket{1 \oplus f(x)} \Big) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big( \ket{x} \ket{1} - \ket{x} \ket{0} \Big) = -\ket{x} \otimes \ket{-}\]

A nifty way to capture this optional negative factor effect, given that MATHI282d31295e30203d2031 and MATHI282d31295e7b317d203d202d31, is:

\[(-1)^{f(x)}\]

And (like we saw with the single qubit version of this problem), our interest in the extra MATHI5c6b65747b2d7d qubit ends at this point because it is unaffected. We can focus on the input MATHI6e-qubit register, which now looks like this:

\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2^n}} \sum_{x = 0}^{2^n - 1} (-1)^{f(x)} \ket{x}\]

It’s starting to look a bit garbled, but it’s just saying that the state is the sum of MATHI325e6e different vector terms that have been flipped to negative if MATHI66287829203d2031 for term MATHI78. For example, if MATHI6e203d2033 then there are MATHI38 terms represented by MATHI5c6b65747b787d in the sum, such as MATHI5c6b65747b3030307d, MATHI5c6b65747b3030317d, MATHI5c6b65747b3031307d, and so on up to MATHI5c6b65747b3131317d. If MATHI662831303129203d2031, then the MATHI5c6b65747b3130317d term will be negative in the sum. And then all will be scaled down by MATHI312f5c737172747b387d to make it unitary.

As if it weren’t garbled enough, the last step is (as before) to apply Hadamard one more time. As we saw above, when we apply it to an all-zeros state MATHI5c6b65747b3030305c646f74737d, the result is an expansion containing a term for every bit pattern. Well, now we’re applying it to the sum of terms for every bit pattern. If you’re into coding, this is what you might call a nested loop. Again, supposing MATHI6e203d2033, we have a sum of MATHI38 terms, some positive, some negative, and each of those will now expand out into MATHI38 terms, some positive, some negative, so we’ll have MATHI3634 terms. But these can then be grouped together because there will be MATHI38 repetitions of MATHI5c6b65747b3030307d, also MATHI38 of MATHI5c6b65747b3030317d, and so on.

Actually multiplying them all out even for MATHI6e203d2033 would be rather tedious. It’s more instructive to think through how each term ends up with its effective final sign. The way Hadamard works on the basis vectors is that it only introduces a negative factor when the input is MATHI5c6b65747b317d, and it only places that negative factor on the output MATHI5c6b65747b317d term. So an all-zeros MATHI5c6b65747b3030305c646f74737d state put through Hadamard produces only positive terms.

With the other terms, those with at least one MATHI31, something remarkable happens: when we group the remaining MATHI3536 multiplied-out terms into their MATHI37 types, among the MATHI38 copies of (say) MATHI5c6b65747b3031307d, MATHI34 are positive and MATHI34 are negative, so they cancel out. This happens for every basis vector apart from all-zeros. This shouldn’t be that surprising though, as we know that Hadamard is self-inverting: MATHI48203d20485e7b2d317d. So that can only mean:

\[H^2 \ket{000\dots} = \ket{000\dots}\]

So if the mystery function is constant, and thus applies the same sign-flip to every term, there are only two possibilities. If MATHI66287829203d2030, there’s no overall sign-flip:

\[H U_f H \ket{000\dots} = \ket{000\dots}\]

Whereas if MATHI66287829203d2031, the sign is flipped:

\[H U_f H \ket{000\dots} = -\ket{000\dots}\]

Either way, this state will with certainty produce a MATHI5c6b65747b307d on every qubit. No other pattern has a non-zero amplitude.

The only other form the mystery function is allowed to take is to be balanced, and I said that was going to seem contrived. What it means for the MATHI5c6b65747b3030305c646f74737d state is that exactly half the terms contributing to it will be positive and half will be negative, and this will be entirely the function’s doing (Hadamard leaves all-zeros states alone.) The first (inner) Hadamard makes a term for every possible value, all of them positive, the mystery function flips the sign of half of them, and the final (outer) Hadamard creates from each a MATHI5c6b65747b3030305c646f74737d contribution that preserves the sign of the term it came from. This means that all the MATHI5c6b65747b3030305c646f74737d contributions cancel out, leaving a zero probability of measuring the all-zeros pattern.

The end result is that a measurement of MATHI5c6b65747b3030305c646f74737d will only happen if it was absolutely certain to happen, because the mystery function is constant. If it is balanced, MATHI5c6b65747b3030305c646f74737d is impossible, so something else will be found (at least one qubit will be in the MATHI5c6b65747b315c646f74737d state.)

Because of the peculiar contrivance of the setup, this is not at all useful. But it demonstrates how a quantum algorithm can produce a deterministic result, and seemingly explore a potentially huge problem space in a simple and practically instantaneous process. With MATHI6e203d20323735 qubits, the number of basis vectors is MATHI325e7b3237357d205c617070726f782031305e7b38327d, about the number of atoms in the visible universe, and yet we seem to be able to probe the behaviour of a function on all of them, all at once.
entry.summary: We ended up being slightly less impressed than we might have been about the Hadamard gate’s ability to narrow down the identity of a mystery function from four possibilities to two with a single measurement, given that we could make the same amount of progress by invoking the function once directly. If you give the function $0$ as the input, it can only output $0$ or $1$, and that divides the four possible functions into two pairs.

entry.title: Quantumania 16 - Diagonal = Easy
entry.content:
A digression before we get back to quantum computing. In our previous linear algebra tomfoolery, something important has been bubbling away, which is the importance of diagonal matrix representation, and what they mean for simplicity. They mean that we can think of the dimensions of the space as being like completely separate, isolated channels, which don’t suffer from any “crosstalk”. It’s like you’re doing several completely independent calculations, with no interference between them.

If you apply MATHI5c6861747b4d7d205c6571756976205c6f70657261746f726e616d657b646961677d284d5f312c204d5f3229 to a vector MATHI5c7665637b767d:

\[\hat{M} \vec{v} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} M_1 & 0 \\ 0 & M_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} M_1 v_1 \\ M_2 v_2 \end{bmatrix}\]

it’s like two completely separate conversations on different phone lines. The MATHI6eth diagonal entry is only applicable to the MATHI6eth coordinate of the vector. If any off-diagonal entry was non-zero it would be a different matter. But diagonal matrices are delightfully straightforward.

We can apply the operator MATHI5c6861747b4d7d twice, and write that as MATHI5c6861747b4d7d5e32:

\[\hat{M}^2 \vec{v} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} M_1 & 0 \\ 0 & M_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} M_1 & 0 \\ 0 & M_2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} v_1 \\ v_2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} M_1^2 v_1 \\ M_2^2 v_2 \end{bmatrix}\]

In a way this is a function applied to the matrix, but the way that works is trivial: we just apply that function to the separate diagonal entries. We can extend this idea to any function MATHI66 (an ordinary mapping between numbers). Such a function can be applied to the matrix as a whole, but it’s really just that we are applying the function separately to the individual diagonal entries.

For matrices in general this wouldn’t make sense: a number-valued function of numbers doesn’t know what to do with a matrix. But with a diagonal matrix, we know the non-zero entries act like independent numbers, so we’re essentially “broadcasting” the function wrapping down to the individual entries:

\[f(M) \equiv \begin{bmatrix} f(M_1) & 0 \\ 0 & f(M_2) \end{bmatrix}\]

This leads to the idea of raising something to the power of an operator. It sounds like gibberish until you realise that as long as the operator can be represented by a diagonal matrix, there’s nothing to it.

What kinds of operator can be represented by a diagonal matrix? The answer to this question depends on what kind of basis we allow. If an operator has eigenvectors that are linearly independent and it has as many as there are dimensions in the space, then we can use the eigenvectors as a basis and represent the operator diagonally.

But for two vectors to be linearly independent just means that they aren’t colinear. We want to be more choosy and require that our basis vectors are orthogonal, because our state vector spaces have an inner product with a simple definition that, in order to produce consistent values regardless of the basis, requires that the basis vectors are orthogonal. So in QM we insist on that, and when we speak of changing the basis, we never mean realigning just some of the basis vectors: they all have to rotate properly together, to stay rigidly orthogonal with each other.

With that restriction, in a real vector space the only kind of operator that can be diagonalised is the kind that scales along orthogonal alignments, and it will be represented in any other allowed basis by a symmetrical matrix.

But in complex vector spaces, it’s a lot more interesting than that. A broader set of operators can be diagonalised in an orthogonal basis. Those that can are called normal operators. Also the test for a normal operator is that it commutes with its adjoint. What do we mean by that?

First, adjoint can be thought of as the abstract geometrical equivalent of the conjugate transpose we’ve been using on matrices. So I could have said, much more verbosely, “If you have an operator, MATHI5c6861747b417d, and you represent it by a matrix MATHI41 in some orthogonal basis, and you take the conjugate transpose of that matrix, and those two matrices commute, then MATHI5c6861747b417d is normal.” Also wherever we talked about hermitian matrices, we could instead have talked about self-adjoint operators.

And second, commuting means that two operators can be applied in either order and the result is the same. Again, dropping down to the matrix representation, if you multiply out the two matrices in both orders, the resulting matrix must be the same either way in order for it to be a normal matrix representing a normal operator:

\[A A^\dagger = A^\dagger A \quad \text{for a normal matrix, A}\]

The surprising thing is that as well as self-adjoint operators being normal, so are unitary operators. Rotations can not generally be diagonalised in a real vector space, but in a complex one they can. How, though? Algebraically it follows automatically from the fact that a unitary operator is defined by the requirement that:

\[U U^\dagger = I\]

That is, the inverse of MATHI55 is its own adjoint. The same must be true going the other way, and so either way around, the result is MATHI49. It commutes with its own adjoint, so unitary implies normal.

Working more intuitively, in a real vector space we know a diagonal matrix scales along orthogonal directions, with the scaling factors given by the diagonal entries themselves. But a unitary operator isn’t allowed to scale along any direction. It preserves the lengths of all vectors as well as the angles between them. So if it has eigenvectors at all, surely their eigenvalues would have to be MATHI5c706d2031. (In fact in the confines of a 2D real vector space, rotations have no eigenvectors, except rotations by a multiple of MATHI5c7069.)

In a complex space, we find the length of a vector MATHI5c6b65747b767d by using the complex form of the inner product, MATHI5c6272616b65747b767d7b767d and then taking the square root. This always gives a real number regardless of whether the vector has complex coordinates. So the eigenvalues of our unitary operator could be complex numbers, as long as they have unit modulus, of the form MATHI655e7b695c74686574617d, lying on the unit circle in the complex plane. The diagonal form of a rotation is like this:

\[\begin{bmatrix} e^{i\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta} \end{bmatrix}\]

The two coordinates rotate in the complex plane in opposite directions. Why is that? The familiar template for a rotation matrix in a real vector space is:

\[\begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta \end{bmatrix}\]

We can imagine the real space MATHI5c6d61746862627b527d5e32 as being embedded within the complex space MATHI5c6d61746862627b437d5e32. That is, the standard basis vectors (the Z basis, to use their qubit names):

\[\ket{0} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad \ket{1} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}\]

are a pair of ingredients that we can scale and sum using only real coordinates, to build any vector that lies within a “real subspace”. To be precise about what we mean by this, to access the whole space with real coordinates, we’d need a couple more weird ingredients:

\[\ket{\gamma} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} i \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad \ket{\kappa} \equiv \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ i \end{bmatrix}\]

This would allow us to build the full range of complex vectors from four real coordinates MATHI28612c20622c20632c206429:

\[\begin{eqnarray*} \ket{\psi} &=& a \ket{0} + b \ket{1} + c \ket{\gamma} + d \ket{\kappa} \\ \\ &\equiv& \begin{bmatrix} a \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ b \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} ci \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ di \end{bmatrix} \\ \\ &=& \begin{bmatrix} a + ci \\ b + di \end{bmatrix} \end{eqnarray*}\]

So we’re still building 2D complex vectors in MATHI5c6d61746862627b437d5e32, but we’re approaching it as a 4D real space MATHI5c6d61746862627b527d5e34, and we can restrict ourselves to a 2D real subspace of that if we like.

If we take a pair of these ingredients that aren’t complex multiples of each other, such as MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI5c6b65747b317d, or MATHI5c6b65747b307d and MATHI5c6b65747b5c6b617070617d, and combine them with complex scalars, we can make any complex vector. So such pairs form a basis for the whole MATHI5c6d61746862627b437d5e32 space, and if we pick an orthogonal, unit-norm pair it’s an orthonormal basis. We can also make other orthonormal bases by linear combination of our ingredients. For example:

\[\ket{v_+} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big[ \ket{0} - \ket{\kappa} \Big] \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -i \end{bmatrix} \quad \quad \ket{v_-} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \Big[ \ket{0} + \ket{\kappa} \Big] \equiv \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ i \end{bmatrix}\]

Why have they been labelled with MATHI2b and MATHI2d in apparent opposition to the sign used in their definitions? Because we’re going to be scaling them by complex phase factors that twist them in the positive (anticlockwise) and negative (clockwise) directions respectively, using the diagonalised rotation matrix defined above.

These two vectors are an orthogonal unit basis, as we can test them with the inner product:

\[\braket{v_+}{v_+} = \braket{v_-}{v_-} = 1\] \[\braket{v_+}{v_-} = 0\]

And we can write down the matrix that would convert a vector expressed in this basis into the standard MATHI5c6b65747b307d2c205c6b65747b317d basis: we just use the definitions of MATHI5c6b65747b765f2b7d and MATHI5c6b65747b765f2d7d as the columns of the matrix:

\[P = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ -i & i \end{bmatrix}\]

It’s easy to show this is unitary (i.e. that MATHI505e5c646167676572203d20505e7b2d317d). With a little more hard labour, leaning on this:

\[e^{i\theta} = \cos \theta + i \sin \theta\]

and being super careful with those minus signs, folks, we can wrap the diagonalised rotation matrix in the usual transform/undo sandwich:

\[P \begin{bmatrix} e^{i\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta} \end{bmatrix} P^\dagger = \begin{bmatrix} \cos \theta & -\sin \theta \\ \sin \theta & \cos \theta \end{bmatrix}\]

So by twisting these two complex basis vectors, MATHI5c6b65747b765f2b7d anticlockwise and MATHI5c6b65747b765f2d7d clockwise, by some phase angle, we have the effect of an ordinary rotation on our embedded real space. This is how an arbitrary rotation can be diagonalised, something that would be impossible in a real vector space.

And as a result, not just one but two of the most important kinds of operator we need in QM can be understood as diagonal matrices, and thus like operations that act independently on separate coordinate channels.
